planting.note: Set divisions or nursery starts in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled to full shade after the soil has warmed; mulch lightly the first winter in colder zones since this species is less cold-hardy than common Ajuga reptans.

directions: Plant rooted offsets in loose, organically enriched soil and keep consistently moist while the mat establishes; unlike Ajuga reptans, this species has deeply cut, jagged-edged foliage and spreads by short stolons rather than long runners, forming a tighter, less invasive carpet. Spikes of violet-blue flowers appear in mid to late spring above the foliage. It suits woodland edges and shaded rock gardens where a slower, well-behaved bugleweed is wanted, but it needs more reliable winter protection than its common cousin in colder climates.

planting.note: Transplant divisions or plugs into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in shade; the trailing stems root at the nodes as they spread, so space plants loosely and let them knit together into a low mat.

directions: Establish in consistently moist, shaded woodland soil where its weak, sprawling stems can root along the ground and knit into an open mat; whorls of narrow leaves release a sweet, hay-like fragrance as they dry, much like true sweet woodruff. Tiny white star-shaped flowers appear in loose clusters in early summer, followed by bristly burr-like seeds that cling to fur and clothing for dispersal. It is a gentle native filler for shaded borders and naturalized woodland plantings, spreading readily but rarely aggressively.

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full to partial shade; give it room to run since it spreads readily by creeping stolons once established.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist soil beneath trees or shrubs, where this East Asian relative of American Meehania cordata forms a semi-evergreen mat of nettle-shaped, scalloped leaves. Whorled spikes of tubular, blue-violet flowers rise above the foliage in late spring, drawing early bumblebees. It spreads steadily by surface stolons to knit together as a weed-suppressing woodland groundcover, and is easily controlled by pulling or trimming runners that stray past their bed.

planting.note: Set divisions into cool, moist, humus-rich forest soil in deep to partial shade; this Pacific Northwest native prefers the same conditions as its eastern relative but forms tighter, less stoloniferous clumps.

directions: Plant in cool, consistently moist, richly organic soil beneath conifers or in shaded ravines, mimicking the deep coastal and montane forests of the Pacific Northwest where it grows. Unlike Tiarella cordifolia, its foliage is typically undivided or only shallowly lobed and it spreads mainly by short rhizomes rather than long runners, forming a slowly expanding clump rather than a running mat. Slender racemes of small, starry white to pinkish flowers rise above the foliage in late spring, followed by attractive foliage that often takes on bronze tones through fall.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or immediately after flowering into cool, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; established clumps resent summer drought more than most Pulmonaria.

directions: Grow in cool, evenly moist, richly organic soil in partial to full shade, where its broad, softly hairy, unspotted grey-green leaves form a dense clump distinct from the silver-spotted lungworts more commonly grown. Clusters of tubular flowers open pink and mature to violet-blue over an extended bloom period in mid to late spring, attracting early bumblebees. It is slower to spread than Pulmonaria saccharata hybrids, staying in a well-mannered clump that suits shaded borders and woodland edges without becoming a running groundcover.
